About These Review Renderings

These passages preserve damaged prose rather than smoothing it into false certainty. They keep OCR loss, embedded cipher tenors, and conjectural readings visible so readers can compare them against the Latin and source scan.

They should be treated as review renderings, not certified final editions.

[Provenance or ownership line:] Ferdinand Albert, [conjectured: Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg].^1

Six Books of the Polygraphy,^2 by Johannes Trithemius,^3 abbot of Peapolis,^4 formerly of Spanheim,^5 addressed to Emperor Maximilian.^6

With favor and privilege [conjectured: of the Imperial Majesty].^7

Johannes Trithemius.^3

A lower caption or subscription after the portrait is [unclear].^8

^1. The OCR “Ferdinando Alberto Dux Frangiscalis et Vicenburgensis” is not a secure dedication formula. “Brunsvicensis et Luneburgensis” is a defensible reconstruction from the ducal style of Brunswick-Lüneburg; the problem is OCR/provenance damage, not authorial obscurity. ^2. Polygraphia: Trithemius’s cryptographic/steganographic “many-writing” work; here the title is not a prose sentence but title-page matter. ^3. Johannes Trithemius (1462-1516), Benedictine abbot and author. The repeated “IO. TRITHEMIVS” is likely a portrait caption/name, not a new imprint statement. ^4. Peapolis is Trithemius’s humanist Latin for Würzburg; “abbas Peapolitanus” means abbot at St James/Würzburg, not Naples. This is an uncommon place-name, not an OCR correction. ^5. Spanheimensis: of Sponheim/Spanheim, Trithemius’s former abbey. ^6. Maximilianus Caesar: Emperor Maximilian I. Latin “ad” means “addressed to / for,” not necessarily a separate personal dedication on this damaged leaf. ^7. The OCR “Lum gratia et privilegio L. OS.” is best read as a damaged “Cum gratia et privilegio C.M.” or similar privilege formula; C.M. would abbreviate Caesarea Maiestas, “Imperial Majesty.” OCR scannos affect initial C/L and abbreviation letters. ^8. The supplied OCR “Lyvolis 1563. m. gris. 2. Ruckius” is not recoverable as Latin from this excerpt and should not be treated silently as a 1563 imprint. Bibliographic controls identify the edition as [Basel]: Haselberg, 1518; see HAB record http://diglib.hab.de/drucke/fb-128/start.htm and LOC record https://www.loc.gov/item/32017914/.

Style C Translation: Clavis Polygraphiae, p. 018 Fragment

Frankish King and Clodius

The most powerful king of the Franks^1 in Germany, in the [conjectured: four-hundred-and-twenty-fourth]^2 year of the Lord’s nativity, when he [conjectured: entered]^3 the borders of the Gauls^4 in force, in order that all things might be done in complete safety, bound foreign minutiae^5 to his secrets.

Clodius the Long-haired,^6 the elder-by-birth son of Pharamund,^7 succeeding his father in the kingship of the Franks, afterward willingly subjected the whole of Gaul to himself and to his rule. He ordered all the Gauls, as conquered men and slaves, to be stripped of their hair and their beards shaved; but he commanded the Franks, conquerors and masters of the Gauls, to let their hair and beard grow. Hence he too was called “the Long-haired.” In imitation of his race, he wrapped the mysteries of his counsel^8 in signs both his own and foreign.

Charlemagne

Charles the Great^9 by surname, [conjectured: the sixty-third]^10 after Marcomer,^11 king of the Franks, who was the first of the Franks to rule the Romans,^12 having Nanno the grammarian^13 as his teacher, and wishing to adorn with grammatical rules the beginnings of Latin in the German language, which was his paternal tongue, undertook a difficult work. Yet, entangled in many matters and overtaken by delay, he did not complete it. But he bound [unclear: bubones?]^14 to various and many minutiae; [unclear], than whom Brabant^15 had no greater [conjectured: native?], nor Germany one at Namur.^16 To the individual prefects of the kingdom he entrusted individual [unclear: bubones?] by art.

Normans and Bede

The Normans,^17 having gone out from the borders of the Goths,^18 when they once cruelly laid waste Gaul, summoned also [unclear: Greek bubones?] and prepared a safe [conjectured: hiding-place / gibbet?]^19 for their secrets, which today is known to few.

Our Bede,^20 a monk in England, not ignorant of the [unclear: secrets? stuffing?]^21 of the Normans, found many things like these in the writings and inventions of the ancients, by which they made a dark path into mysteries. He himself first commended astrology^22 to the memory of posterity, and invented dactylology.^23

There were some who discerned minutiae by visible accidents,^24 for whom prudence did not fear night in the day, and, without the ministry of [unclear: bubones?], light shone in darkness.

Steganography and Later Arts

Concerning these matters of our Steganography,^25 because a certain illustrious count palatine and prince-elector^26 made inquiry, he caused clear documents to be approved for us by experiment. Others, however, multiplying rules by the division of minutiae, [unclear] the schemes of nature back to the beginnings of the barbarians, [unclear] in darkness the shadow-dances^27 of those being born; and where the secrecy of counsel required it, by [conjectured: diagrams]^28 it supplied a cabala^29 to the absent. Great labor lies in these things, and long exercise of a sharp mind; in this no one suddenly becomes skilled at first sight. Necessity suffices for all things.

There were also those whom celestial harmony^30 taught to compose foreign utterances: for those who understood, the vision of these was twofold, while the one [conjectured: held the sense in suspense], the other lifted the mind into the ether. God can do all things. Many have tried to seek light in shadow without light, but by no means could they, because the fire now lies buried in ashes. Some, practiced painters of masks,^31 divided [unclear: twenty?] one into two [unclear: at a point], of whom one [unclear: mirophos] in [unclear].

^1. “Francorũ” = Francorum. OCR abbreviation expansion; named people of the Franks. ^2. OCR “quadragesimaetimo uicefimo quarto” is not grammatical as printed; likely a damaged numeral such as “quadringentesimo vicesimo quarto,” i.e. 424. ^3. OCR “in traraet” is probably “intraret.” Positional spacing and letter confusion. ^4. “Gallorum” / Gauls; historical-ethnic vocabulary. ^5. “minutiae” is retained as a technical steganographic/cipher term in this passage; it seems to denote small units, signs, or cipher elements. ^6. Clodius Crinitus, a legendary/early Frankish ruler; “Crinitus” means long-haired. ^7. Pharamund/Pharamond, legendary king of the Franks; OCR “Pharamidi” for Pharamundi. ^8. “mysteria consilii” is secrecy/counsel vocabulary; in Trithemius this often shades into steganographic concealment. ^9. OCR “Caro Ius Magnus” = Carolus Magnus, Charlemagne. ^10. OCR “faxegeminus” is likely a scanno for a numeral such as “sexagesimus”; the exact ordinal remains uncertain. ^11. Marcomer/Marcomir, legendary Frankish ancestor or ruler. ^12. “Imperavit Romanis” refers to Charlemagne’s imperial rule over Romans/the Roman Empire. ^13. “Nannone grammatico” may refer to an otherwise uncertain grammarian; the name is preserved but should be checked against the print. ^14. OCR repeatedly gives “bubones” / “bur bonibus” / “But bones.” It may be a scanno or a deliberately odd cipher term; not safely normalized. ^15. Brabant, historical region in the Low Countries. ^16. Normans; historical-military people. ^18. “Goths” here is ethnic/geographical vocabulary, possibly legendary ethnography. ^19. OCR “laibulum” could be “latibulum” (hiding-place) or, less likely, “patibulum” (gibbet); context favors “latibulum,” but the reading is not secure. ^20. Bede, the English monk and scholar. ^21. OCR “far ci” is not secure; possibly a scanno for a word meaning secrets, art, or practice. ^22. Astrology as a learned/technical art. ^23. Dactylology: finger-sign language or finger-reckoning/signing, a technical communication term. ^24. “accidentia visibilia” are visible accidental features/signs; scholastic and technical vocabulary. ^25. Steganography: Trithemius’s art of hidden writing; OCR “fleganographie” for steganographiae. ^26. “comes palatinus princeps elector” = count palatine and prince-elector, likely the Palatine elector; named title, not identified further from this fragment. ^27. OCR “orchemata” resembles Greek-derived “orchemata,” dances; phrase remains authorially obscure and OCR-damaged. ^28. OCR “diapryamata” may point to “diagrammata,” diagrams, but the reading is conjectural. ^29. Cabala/Kabbalah, esoteric technical term; here probably a method of concealed communication to absentees. ^30. “harmonia coelestis,” celestial harmony; theological/esoteric cosmological vocabulary. ^31. “larvarum pictores,” painters of masks/phantoms; obscure, possibly a cipher-art metaphor rather than literal painters.

Style C Translation: Clavis Polygraphiae, Indices to Books III-V

Index of the things which [conjectured: the third] book of the Polygraphy contains^1

In the third book of the Polygraphy, after crossing the prescribed boundaries of our nation [unclear: or mode/reason of speech], we are led to foreign things; and, being set in the midst of the French in an [unclear: essential/native] way,^2 we wander further through the images and likenesses of barbarian peoples.^3 For with almost four thousand mythological phrase-units^4 set in order by art, we very easily show the force of an artificial unity,^5 and how symbolic signs,^6 with their own binary, may conceal it more safely at every time. Here the binary is harder for unity; and unless our philologist is made sharp-sighted by prudence, he will render the binary as contrary to the monad.^7 For only the ternary, which proceeds from unity and the binary, [unclear: gives/contains] in itself the [unclear] of both.^8 What if the necessary usefulness of the method^9 is extended beyond the bounds of the proposed matter, and so many paraphrases^10 were to strive through the minutes from the beginning of the day, until the minute establishes the degree at which night [unclear: equals] day? The face of this image [unclear: knows the favor/propitiousness] of silence; it does not fear the frauds of [unclear]. However greatly you wish to extend the supply, it is varied without end.

Index, or [unclear: depiction/painting], of the things treated in the fourth book

In the fourth book of the Polygraphy we have much more fully brought the binary, a matter beset by many obstacles, back to unity at first sight and without laborious difficulties. Hence we use a circle^11 in great matters, a line or point in the smallest. Nor does it matter whether [unclear: day] does not surpass [unclear], or whether light does not yield to darkness, because the circle admits no end, and fullness is not admired in empty things. For they are contraries, and when one succeeds, the other is corrupted by the other. The singular mystery of the binary code^12 is transmitted in this fourth book of the Polygraphy, while [unclear: the old copyist/older abundance itself] otherwise [unclear] more copiously, unless it is marked in the height by the binary. But in that part, among [unclear: owls/obscurities], lightness is for us [unclear] in difficult suspicions. The joining-together of this matter makes paraphrases from infinite atoms.

Index, or [unclear: depiction/painting], of the things treated in the fifth book

In the fifth book of the Polygraphy, the letters of the Latins,^13 which we Germans also use,^14 [are arranged] in order in two tables, of which one is called [conjectured: the straight table], and the other [conjectured: the inverse].^15 To these we have added [unclear: old arrangements/figures], so that in foreign matters, and with less labor than in open ones, we may seem to work without difficulty. For besides those things which have been placed by us in plain sight, many more still lie hidden in the inner secrets; through them a way is opened for the understanding operator^16 toward greater things than those which are put before the eyes of the unskilled. We have also added [unclear: universal grammar/rules], by which, according to our will, hidden things may become manifest. Hence, through the [unclear: full/formal] operation of this book, all [unclear: beginnings/unknown things] are safely handed over to cabalistic methods,^17 although the mysteries [unclear: are protected/are made new] from the suspicion of [unclear]. For the very form of the metathesis of signs^18 generates suspicion in the beholder, though no harm was present in it for [unclear: owls/the ignorant]. But you, once you have attained the understanding of this work, will easily penetrate every metathesis of letters among our people and among the Latins.

This likely concerns French-language material in Book III. ^3. OCR “filiúdines bar baronú lógiús cuagamur” is recoverable as “similitudines barbarorum longius vagamur.” “Barbarian” here means non-Latin/foreign, not necessarily savage. ^4. “phra[m]atib[?]” appears to be “phrasmatibus/phrasematis,” phrase-units or formulaic expressions used for polygraphic substitution. ^5. “unitas artificialis” is technical cipher language: an artificial unifying system for diverse signs or phrases. ^6. “notíes” likely for “notae,” signs/marks, not “notions” in the modern abstract sense. ^7. Clavis Polygraphiae, Preface / Decipherment Commentary, Page 027

[conjectured: Whoever] has learned to read and write in his mother tongue^1 is taught, under the Latin language, how to write as he wishes, elegantly and [conjectured: concisely]; how by solitary [conjectured: notes]^2 to conceal and hide the secrets of his hidden signifying-system^3; how, by whatever silent art^4 he chooses, to announce matters very widely, safely, securely, and without suspicion; and likewise to forewarn [unclear], so that they may not be understood by others [unclear]. This we promise.

The third benefit is that to one unskilled in Roman speech^5 we promise that in a few hours he will not only [conjectured: be able] to write and read, but also to understand, if he prudently applies the duty of the office; this we have judged should not be rejected without reasonable cause. For the novice pupil of this new art^6 will write what he had known in his own language, and, once it has been governed by instruction in the Latin tongue, [conjectured: he will understand the cosmopolitan/interpreted speech], if you take it word by word; that will suffice for use. Finally, this instruction can be enlarged to all the affairs and business of the world. How those things can be done, if anyone wishes to hear it from me, he must first [conjectured: sow] such seeds of speech^7 as he has received and merited. For all things are not owed to all people, but one person is to be preferred to another.

The fourth benefit is that, by enlargement of the received likeness of the thing, all those things can be extended into any language whatever, once the binary instruction^8 has been reduced to unity. Yet this is not granted to just any people one can name, but only to those persons whom God, by his special grace, and art and nature, have dignified for such things.

The fifth benefit is that, by imitation of likeness, those skilled in the art can devise, through the invention of our science, whatever secrets of our mind we wish to have hidden, in many and manifold ways, by such methods that by no other person from outside will they ever be able to be noticed. A manifold speech without voice^9 is given to them; through it, safely, securely, very widely, with every suspicion removed, we shall be able to indicate most fully to those who know the art all conceptions of our mind, whatever their difficulty. And this wonderful invention has innumerable developments, capable of every kind of mystery.^10

The sixth benefit is that, through understanding this work, you will be able to discover a free [conjectured: method of] metathesis,^11 regulated by literary transposition,^12 and nevertheless to form it in such a way that it serves only those who know the art, and absolutely no other person in the world. Great is the power of metathesis, both in form and operation; it has many modes and is varied in many ways.

The seventh benefit is that, through understanding this volume, a very great faculty is given to those desiring to enlarge [conjectured: it] without labor of memory, whenever the small seeds^7 have been placed in their proper degrees. For a good reason all things are hidden and concealed, wrapped in accepted words and figures; if anyone wishes to understand them fully, let him recall to mind [conjectured: that unremitting labor conquers all things]. For it will have been enough for me to have set down some few principles and to have handed on modest elements of symbolic striking/writing^13, rough and deliberately unformed. For there was neither time nor reason for our discoveries to be shaped with more refinement; nor did the authority of one [unclear] publish them for boys to become indignant at. [unclear] All things are untimely which do not agree with the customs and the time of the mortals among whom they are produced.

Page 027

Many very noble human talents have belonged to unsuitable times, and many new things are found almost in times not their own. What did the remarkable invention in nautical art^14 profit the outstanding [conjectured: Bartholomaeus]^15, under Pope Innocent VIII?^16 In a certain little book he offered it for sale for several thousand ducats; yet neither the pontiff himself, nor the Venetians, nor the Genoese,^17 to whom the matter thus proposed [conjectured: he had made over / submitted] in due manner, deigned to meet with him. For he promised that by his art he could preserve thirty ships in the middle of the sea, repair a broken one, and retrieve without danger whatever had been cast into the depths. But no one took care. Nor does it escape me that many, with Naso,^18 have perished by their own genius. Therefore it is better to set a limit to knowledge than, without [conjectured: advantage], to expose oneself to the hatred and detraction of many, among whom it is customary to despise anything which they have not learned.

Johannes Trithemius to the Reader: Numeral Letters

Address

Johannes Trithemius,^1 abbot [unclear: PEAPQ / LITANVS],^2 sends greeting to the reader.

Prefatory Explanation

Since the letters of the Greeks^3 and Hebrews^4 are all numeral, I have often wondered that the curious Latin usage of the ancients did not also make its own letters subscribe to numbering. The Hebrews, by doubling certain letters [unclear], established twenty-eight signs sufficient for every number. The Greeks also, because of a defect in [their] letters, supplied it with like prudence by the addition of four characters.

Since we, therefore, have twenty-four letters, why do we not also make our letters numeral? Likewise we can discover four doubled forms. Let us give four in examples, and this will be enough for every number: final m and n [unclear]; likewise final r and s; likewise long f and final or closed s; likewise closed v and open u.^5 When these are added to the twenty-four usual letters, we shall have twenty-eight characters sufficient for all numbers.

Therefore it is no matter of great labor to grasp the business of numbering and the method, for those who know these letters, if they have once commended them to memory. For this brief invention of ours can be useful to many, since with few letters it embraces many thousands in number; all these can be discerned and understood at first sight, more clearly than light, without any calculation. This, especially in large numbers, seems to many persons less experienced in the art of calculation not to be so easily possible by the figures of algorism.^6 For as soon as you have cast your eye on a number, however great, you will be able both to understand it fully and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. And so that this may be easy, we shall gather together the letters themselves reduced to number. Written 16 March, in the year 1507.^7

The sixth book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius,^1 abbot of Saint James the Greater the Apostle at Würzburg,^2 begins.

Before every invention and use of letters,^3 at the beginning of the world, when human beings were still uncultivated in intellect and morals, [conjectured: under the alternating rule] of the first three [conjectured: intelligences],^4 as some suppose, succeeding one another in order for one thousand and sixty-three years,^5 they were, in the sphere of the planets,^6 present in their own way to bodily things on earth through their influences.

The ancient speculators on this matter say that Saturn,^7 from the beginning of the world, presided chiefly by influence over things germinating and being born on earth, with his own ruling intelligence moderating him: this intelligence they called Orifiel,^8 that is, [conjectured: “the life-maker / life-giver of God”], for three hundred fifty-four lunar years, likewise four months, and just as many days and hours. We report these things as poetic matters; we do not affirm them. After Saturn, Venus; after Venus, the lordship of Jove is set down as assumed. After Jove, Mercury,^9 fourth in order, as ruler, adorned the minds of human beings with various arts.

Under the three intelligences just mentioned, namely while Saturn, Venus, and Jove^10 were ruling, they assert that human beings did not have the use or knowledge of letters. Hence, whenever one person wished to announce something secret to another, he did not do it in written characters, since the office of letters was lacking, but by certain likenesses of animals, trees, and plants, or of other sensible things, according as those who had agreed among themselves did it symbolically.^11

The age of Saturn, as they say, gave human beings habits suited to the property of its influence. For it made them farmers, hunters, founders of cities,^12 rough, [conjectured: forest-dwelling], sad, simple, uncultivated in life and morals, and living a long time in the flesh. After Orifiel of Saturn, as those who hold such opinions say, the intelligence Anael,^13 mover of Venus, acquired [conjectured: the influence of the sphere] for three hundred fifty-four years [unclear: text breaks at page boundary].

Clavis Polygraphiae, decipherment commentary / preface, pp. 496-499

Damaged Opening

Even if the characters are not sufficiently beautiful and elegant, and [unclear], nevertheless it pleased me to join them, along with the new inventions of mine set down above, for the honor and reverence due to antiquity,^1 since there was no one, however slightly industrious, who could not devise prettier ones for himself according to his own judgment. Therefore this misshapen crookedness of writing [unclear] by continuous practice in writing, by easy correction, will be able to amend, and, by frequent exercise, make pleasing through habit.

Page 496

For no one, however learned or educated in any language, becomes even a good scribe^2 unless, through long habit of writing, he has changed practice into art. Another follows.

[Cipher alphabet / character table follows.]

If anyone wishes, according to his own judgment, to fashion a new alphabet^3 for himself, two things above all must be observed; yet I do not always find these preserved in the foregoing examples. First, that he form characters easy to draw, and the simpler they are, the better they will be. Second, that he so arrange the individual letters that, when they are joined together into words, they present a beautiful and elegant face. I add a third point, not previously promised: if you wish the writing to remain secret, make some letters of the alphabet double, in the manner of the Hebrews.^4

Alphabet of Hichus, Ancient Bard of the Franks

[Cipher alphabet / character table follows.]

This Hichus^5 the Frank is said to have come with Marcomer^6 from the borders of Scythia^7 to [unclear] Rhine in Germany, and to have invented these characters as a supplement to the German language; they seem to agree with it well enough in several respects.

Pharamund^8 also, king of the Franks in Germany, the forty-third after Marcomer, who had brought in the people, died in the [conjectured: forty-sixth] year of the Lord’s nativity; when, for the purpose of invading Gaul,^9 he sent out his scouts, he found that they were writing among themselves in such characters as these.

the order of our usual alphabet, the letters themselves changed in an unusual way, and we shall have made a rather beautiful and elegant secret and mystical way of writing. [Letter-number table follows.]

Once these principles of numbering with our letters have been rightly understood, it will now be easy to carry the number to any progression whatever, just as has been shown plainly enough in the preceding books. Now let us arrange an alphabet from these.

You now have, from Latin letters, a foreign alphabet of the kind which, as we said above, the Northmen once made for themselves from Greek letters. ^1. “Antiquity” here means the alleged ancient authority of the alphabets; the opening line is OCR-damaged, so the precise predicate after “beautiful and elegant” is not recoverable from this copy. ^2. Latin “scriptor” can mean writer, scribe, or copyist; here the practical art of pen-forms and handwriting is in view. ^3. “Alphabetum” in Trithemius includes artificial, cipher, and substitution alphabets, not merely ordinary ABC order. ^4. “After the manner of the Hebrews” refers to the use of duplicate or variant letter forms; the OCR “bebraeorum” is a scanno for “Hebraeorum.” ^5. “Hichus” is the printed/OCR form here; the surrounding title “HICHI” suggests a legendary Frankish “vates,” but the name should not be normalized silently. ^6. Marcomer is a legendary early Frankish leader in medieval and early-modern Frankish origin narratives. ^7. Scythia is a conventional learned toponym for northeastern/eastern barbarian origins, not a precise modern geography. ^8. Pharamund/Faramund is a legendary king of the Franks; the chronology in the OCR line is corrupt and historically fabulous. ^9. Gaul: Latin “Galli”/“Gallia” in this damaged sentence; OCR around the invasion clause is badly distorted. ^10. “Nortmanni” means Northmen/Normans; the OCR repeatedly gives recoverable letter-confusions in this word. ^11. Bede is invoked as an authority for an alphabetic form; no claim is made here that the attribution is historically secure. ^12. Clavis Polygraphiae, Decipherment Commentary / Preface

First Expansion Table

[The preceding alphanumeric table is a cipher table and is not translated here; its OCR state is preserved in the source.]^1

We do not expand the [conjectured: orbemata / cipher-wheels],^2 since a reason moves us: because, when it is driven farther with its own progression,^3 the immeasurable labor terrifies the mind. As for the unity,^4 which, by design, we passed over without placing it, we judge that it must be set before our additions in due order. For from those six things which we have shown by way of example, whoever is fit [conjectured: in understanding]^5 will easily attain greater things. All things are conveyed by hidden means.^6

Page 507

Second table of anomalous expansion.^7

Whoever wishes to observe the rule of the [conjectured: orbema / cipher-wheel],^2 will have an easy and ready method of writing, and likewise of reading, the things that are secret. But whoever has transgressed the norm of the art,^8 will have toil along with his wish.

Clavis Polygraphiae / Polygraphia Closing Matter

Closing Exhortation

[unclear: many] mysteries, and the greater [conjectured: things] you will have found from these, the more ample are those that remain to be found. A road is being prepared for beginners; for those advancing along it, it will not be difficult, in the course of time, to find many things, rare things, and very great things.^1 Here one who did not know how will learn to write Latin, and prudently to wrap almost all the mysteries of his own will in a foreign [conjectured: form or idiom].^2

But so that one may understand not merely his own such mysteries which he has wrapped up [unclear: idiosa], but may also disclose the open ones, of which he has almost always until now been ignorant, the business is not one of great labor, if the paraphraser [or interpreter] of ours in this volume has fully grasped the intention.^3 For beneath the bark lie the kernels of our steganography, buried for a just reason, lest it feed unworthy babblers.^4

Indeed it had been [conjectured: foreseen / arranged] in the work that one man should not publish the work to another, but that it should be distributed by its own use alone and [unclear]. Having been wearied after a long navigation, we set our anchor here, under the name of Jesus Christ, savior of the faithful,^5 on the twenty-first day of the month of March,^6 in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1508,^7 in the eleventh Roman indiction,^8 at Paspoli [conjectured: Paspol?], a city of eastern Francia, which they also call Würzburg and Herbipolis.^9

End Of The Sixth Book

The end of the sixth book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius,^10 abbot at Saint James in Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim,^11 of the order of the divine father Benedict,^12 is present.

Imprint

Printed with the money and at the expense of the most upright bookseller Johannes Haselberg of Aia, in the diocese of Constance,^13 in the year 1518, in the month of July.

Title Page Of The Clavis

Key of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of divine James at Herbipolis, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, of the observance of the Bursfeld fathers.^14 With privilege that it not be printed or sold by another for ten years, under the penalty as set forth in the letters. Johannes Trithemius.

^1. “prosescentibus,” “discile,” and “fucessu” are OCR scannos for proficientibus, difficile, and successu. ^2. “peregrino” is syntactically under-supplied in the OCR text; it likely means a foreign idiom, style, or disguise rather than a foreign person. ^3. “para phrastes nos tram” is recoverable as paraphrastes nostram/noster, an interpreter or paraphraser; the grammar remains damaged. “affectus inté tionem” is probably assecutus intentionem or similar, but not certain. ^4. Steganographia is Trithemius’s technical term for hidden writing. “blatteronibus” appears to mean babblers/chatterers; the form may be authorial or corrupt. ^5. Jesus Christ is named in the formal Christian dating/colophon formula. ^6. “mensis Martis” is an OCR or print form for mensis Martii, March. ^7. The stated completion date is March 21, 1508. ^8. The Roman indiction was a fifteen-year fiscal dating cycle used in medieval and early-modern documents. ^9. “Paspoli Francoru orientalisu” is heavily corrupt. “Vuiricburg” and “Herbipolim” identify Würzburg / Herbipolis in eastern Francia. ^10. Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), Benedictine abbot and author of the Polygraphia and Steganographia. ^11. Sponheim: Trithemius’s former abbey before his Würzburg period. ^12. The Order of Saint Benedict, the monastic order to which Trithemius belonged. ^13. Johannes Haselberg of Aia is the named bookseller/financier of the 1518 printing; “Constantiensis diocesis” is the diocese of Constance. ^14.
